clue.text: Leaves a quid

definitions.meaning: the dried leaves of a plant that are smoked, chewed or taken as snuff
a quid is also a lump of something chewed, especially a plug of the leaf held in the cheek

explanation.surface: Someone walks off and leaves behind a pound coin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quid' looks like British slang for a pound; here it is the chewing sense, a wad of the leaf held in the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaf crop is dried and sold for smoking and chewing, and a chewed plug of it is called a quid.

clue.text: It's assumed flyer accepts current

indicators.note: a bird that accepts something takes it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a tit is a small bird, a flyer
AC stands for alternating current

explanation.surface: Someone takes it for granted that a pilot will be fine with electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tacit is understood without being said, that is, assumed or implied.

clue.text: A Slav rising, with Langley's support, in Italy

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath the one before it
in a down clue a word that rises is read from the bottom up, so backwards

parts.note: a Serb is a Slav
Langley, Virginia is the headquarters of the CIA, so the agency is Langley's

explanation.surface: An Eastern European uprising in Italy is backed by American intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'A' is only the article. 'Rising' turns SERB upward to BRES; 'support' puts CIA beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: Brescia is a city in Lombardy, so it is a place to be found in Italy.

clue.text: How potential winners go back to front

definitions.text: How potential winners go back to front

parts.words: How potential winners go back to front
parts.note: a contender who wins late moves from the rear of the field to the lead, from back to front

explanation.surface: Describes how a likely winner might make progress in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back to front' looks like a reversal signal, but it literally describes a runner moving up from last place to first.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes overtaking from a losing position to win, which is going from back to front.

clue.text: Rock singer's prayer upsetting Ebenezer Scrooge: "No good! My old BMW'd 'aunt you!"

indicators.note: upsetting knocks the letters out of order, so they are rearranged
No means without, so the letter for good is removed from the words before

parts.note: taken as written, the d of BMW'd counting as a letter
taken as written, the dropped h of haunt not counted

explanation.surface: A miser responds to a rock star's plea with the threat that his old car will haunt them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No good' deletes the G of SCROOGE, leaving EBENEZERSCROOE; with MYOLDBMWD and AUNTYOU that makes 30 letters, which 'upsetting' rearranges. The song is Janis Joplin's mock prayer for a luxury car.
explanation.definitionFit: Janis Joplin's song opens as a prayer to the Lord asking for a luxury German car.

clue.text: Was bent on giving the setter an outrageous kickback

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me

indicators.note: a kickback here is a kick going backwards, so the word for outrageous is read in reverse

parts.note: OTT, over the top, means outrageous

explanation.surface: Someone was determined to give the crossword compiler a scandalous bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kickback' looks like a bribe, but it is a backwards kick that turns only the word for outrageous round. 'Giving' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To have meant to do something is to have intended or been set on doing it.

clue.text: See 4
No lover of shopkeepers?

parts.note: Napoleon is said to have dismissed England as a nation of shopkeepers, so someone who dislikes the shopkeepers dislikes the English

explanation.surface: Describes someone who doesn't care for retailers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'nation of shopkeepers' jibe, credited to Napoleon, is the key: the shopkeepers are the English.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hostile to England and the English is a person with no love for that nation.

clue.text: Something of Bloody Mary Tudor's opener: "Down with French pacifist!"

indicators.note: a word's opener is its first letter

parts.note: the French cry for down with is a bas
CO is a conscientious objector, one who refuses to fight

explanation.surface: Queen Mary I's first words are a cry against a French peacenik.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody Mary' looks like the Tudor queen, but it is the vodka and tomato cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: The hot pepper sauce is a standard ingredient of a Bloody Mary cocktail, so it is something of one.

clue.text: Dictionary work: nothing going for one solver of the Sphinx's riddle

parts.note: the OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

indicators.note: one thing going for another is swapped in exchange for it

parts.note: an opus is a work
O looks like zero, nothing
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A lexicographer's work in which nothing goes to help the one who solves the Sphinx's puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing going for one' swaps the O of OPUS for I, giving IPUS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Oedipus answered the riddle of the Sphinx at Thebes.

clue.text: Comrades! A revolution here in pop!

indicators.note: a revolution turns everything over, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rallying call to fellow revolutionaries announcing an uprising in the drinks world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here in' is a link to the definition. 'Pop' looks like music but is a fizzy drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream soda is a sweet vanilla-flavoured fizzy drink, a kind of pop.

clue.text: Corrupt man from Spithead, as it were

annotationWithheld.why: Corrupt man from Spithead, as it were (2,3): 'Corrupt' defines GO BAD, but no parse of 'man from Spithead, as it were' to GOBAD could be confirmed (GOB, spit or sailor, accounts for three letters at most) and no blog or clue database has it
annotationWithheld.clue: Corrupt man from Spithead, as it were

clue.text: Take in food

definitions.meaning: to take in a garment is to make it narrower by folding a pleat
British schoolchildren's slang for food, especially sweets and snacks

explanation.definitionFit: A tailor folds fabric in to take in a dress, and British school slang calls snacks by the same word.

clue.text: Nothing to do with dishing the dirt?

definitions.text: Nothing to do with dishing the dirt?

parts.words: Nothing to do with dishing the dirt?
parts.note: reads as something unrelated to scandal, but splits as nothing to do, meaning unoccupied, together with dishing the dirt, meaning spreading scandal

explanation.surface: Asks whether something is unconnected with scandal-mongering.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface denies any link with gossip, but 'Nothing to do' means unoccupied and 'with' joins it to the gossiping.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle gossip is chatter about others from people with nothing better to do.

clue.text: See 3
German chap heard to perform work of Sassoon

indicators.note: heard means the word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: Herr is the German for Mr, a German gentleman
to do is to perform

explanation.surface: A German man is overheard acting out a piece by the war poet Siegfried Sassoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sassoon' suggests the war poet Siegfried Sassoon; it is Vidal Sassoon, the celebrity hairdresser.
explanation.definitionFit: Vidal Sassoon was a famous hairdresser, so a styled cut is his kind of work.

clue.text: Who's heard in musical partnership?

parts.note: an owl's call sounds like who, and such calls are hoots, so the who of owls is heard as hoots in a word for partnership

explanation.surface: Asks which band is heard performing in a musical double act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who' looks like the rock band; it is the call of an owl, a hoot, and to be 'in' the answer is to be in league.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in cahoots means being in close partnership or collusion with someone.

clue.text: The soft touch that purifies the soul, say

definitions.meaning: a person who is easily put upon, a pushover
a mat at the threshold cleans the soles of shoes, with soul standing for sole by sound

explanation.surface: Something gentle that cleanses the spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soul, say' is a sound-alike for sole: the mat cleans the soles of the feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who lets others walk all over them is likened to the mat by the front door.

clue.text: Set down traveller to reach the Land of Nod?

definitions.meaning: to let a passenger out of a vehicle
to fall asleep, the Land of Nod being a jocular name for sleep

explanation.surface: Leave a passenger and then fall asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver lets a passenger out at a stop, and a tired person falls asleep: both senses share the phrase.

clue.text: Loner who'd tell more porkies than others, right?

definitions.meaning: someone who stands apart from the rest

definitions.text: who'd tell more porkies than others, right?
definitions.meaning: porkies, from pork pies, is rhyming slang for lies, so one who out-lies the rest is read as a whimsical noun

explanation.surface: Asks whether the solitary type is the biggest liar of all.
explanation.walkthrough: Porkies is British rhyming slang: pork pies = lies. The second reading splits the answer as OUT-LIER, one who lies more.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlier is someone or something set apart from the main group, a loner.

clue.text: See 27
I'm a popular banker, coming up with the folding!

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written
the Giro, the Post Office's Girobank, was the people's bank

explanation.surface: A friendly bank employee announces that the crease is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming up' reverses the whole run IMAGIRO. Girobank was the Post Office's bank, a popular high street banker in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding.

clue.text: Where the slate is used and when it is not

definitions.meaning: roof slates are laid on top of a building
a drink not put on the slate, the tab, is one given free by the landlord

explanation.surface: Contrasts roofing material with a pub tab.
explanation.walkthrough: A pub 'slate' is a running tab of what a customer owes; drinks given free are not put on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Slates go on top of a building, and a free drink from the bar is said to be given by the pub.

clue.text: Brief briefs maker?

definitions.meaning: a brief is a barrister, and a senior barrister in Britain is called by the name of the fabric
a fabric from which underwear briefs are made

explanation.surface: A short note about an underwear manufacturer.
explanation.walkthrough: A brief is a barrister; a Queen's Counsel 'takes silk' and is known as a silk. The second sense is the cloth used for briefs.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior British barrister wears a gown of the fabric, and luxury underwear is made from it.

clue.text: Greek character heard to tell better jokes?

indicators.note: heard means the word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: to cap a joke is to top it, and one who does so is a capper

explanation.surface: A Greek person is overheard trying to outdo others with jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' is a letter of the Greek alphabet, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Kappa is the tenth letter of the Greek alphabet, a character in that script.

clue.text: Lok Sabah recessing with a toast to the Rikstag

indicators.note: in a down clue going into recess is taken as retreating backwards up the column
with means the answer is held within the words before

explanation.surface: India's lower house goes into recess as Sweden's parliament is toasted.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lok Sabha is India's lower house of parliament. Read LOKSABAH backwards as HABASKOL and the answer sits at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Skol is the Scandinavian drinking toast, cheers, fitting for the Swedish parliament.

clue.text: Ring the wife! One earned a buck

parts.note: O is ring-shaped
rib is jocular for a wife, from Eve made from Adam's rib
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone told to phone their wife, having earned a dollar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buck' looks like a dollar; it is a male antelope. 'Earned' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The oribi is a small African antelope, and a male one is a buck.

clue.text: Up sticks and pack m' bare essentials!

indicators.note: reducing things to their essentials breaks them up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to move on, taking only the bare minimum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up sticks' is British for moving house. 'Essentials' rearranges PACKMBARE.
explanation.definitionFit: To up sticks is to move away, and campers do so when they take down their tents.

clue.text: Distant daughter supplants wife of electromagnetic Michael

indicators.note: one thing supplanting another takes its place, so a letter is swapped

parts.note: faraway means distant

explanation.surface: A daughter living far away takes the place of a famous scientist's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' is a link. 'Daughter supplants wife' swaps the W in FARAWAY for D.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Faraday was the scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction.

clue.text: Beerbohm drowned her suitors in polluted bio-lake. Zounds!

indicators.note: polluted water is fouled and stirred up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A heroine's admirers are drowned in a dirty lake, to an oath of astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: In Max Beerbohm's 1911 novel the Oxford beauty drives all her undergraduate suitors to drown themselves. 'Zounds' is an old oath.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the title heroine of Max Beerbohm's novel, whose admirers all drown for love of her.
